newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean won falls on trade deficit, dlr/yen rise.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean won falls on trade deficit, dlr/yen rise.

text.p: The South Korean won's steep decline against the dollar might boost exports, but a further depreciation could batter a stock market desperately in need of fund inflows from abroad, analysts said on Monday.
The won dropped to 867.80 to the dollar on Monday, its lowest level since a market-average system was introduced in March 1990. It later rose on the central bank's dollar sales.
It closed trading at 866.90, down from the previous close at 864.90 on Friday, after touching the day's high of 864.40.
The won lost about eight percent against the greenback in 1996, and fell another two percent in January because of a widening trade deficit and the dollar's strength against the Japanese yen.
The dollar climbed about four percent against the yen in January.

"The won's drop will contribute to correcting the nation's trade deficit by boosting exports," said a trade ministry official. "But benefits from the cheap won will be offset in many areas by the faster drop of the Japanese yen."
South Korean exporters compete with Japanese rivals in their major export markets for products ranging from semiconductors and electronic appliances to ships and motor vehicles.
South Korea posted a record monthly trade deficit of $3.48 billion in January, after it suffered a record annual shortfall of $20.38 billion in calendar 1996.
But a tumbling won could batter the Seoul stock market by frightening off foreign investors from buying South Korean shares in fear of foreign exchange losses, stock market analysts said.

"Foreign investors are worried the won's drop will result in currency translation losses when the market is unlikely to rebound significantly," said Namuh Rhee, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities in Seoul.
The Seoul stock market has languished since last May under pressure from fears that demand for stocks would trail new share supply during a slowing economy.
The composite index closed Monday's trading at 687.25 points, down more than 30 percent from 986.84 hit on May 7.
Analysts said the government was expected to offer incentives to encourage inflow of foreign funds to help make up for dollar shortages created by the trade deficit.

They said the government was seen looking for the timing of a planned expansion of the foreign share ownership limit. South Korea has said it would raise the ceiling to 23 percent this year from 20 percent, and by a further three percentage points in 1998 and 1999.
But analysts said artificial steps to bring in foreign funds could lead to increased pressure on inflation and interest rates, that would further discourage foreign investment.

They said foreign investment had been affected by the Hanbo Group's financial crisis and nearly a month of labour unrest sparked by controversial labour law that was pushed through parliament in December.
Four of Hanbo Group units, including the group's flagship Hanbo Steel Co, are seeking court receivership after the steelmaker defaulted on debt repayments late last month.
The Bank of Korea has forecast this year's consumer inflation at 4.7 percent, against a 4.5 percent rise in 1996.
